title: Knitted snood
subtitle: A hairnet-style neckwarmer worked flat and seamed into a short wide tube.
excerpt: A snood knitted flat in 1x1 rib on 5 mm needles with worsted-weight yarn, seamed into a short wide tube, finishing at 70 cm circumference and 30 cm tall. The snood is wide enough to pull up over the hair as well as worn as a neckwarmer, and the rib makes the fabric stretchy and reversible.
sourceNotes: Knitted snoods appear in Weldon's Practical Knitter (1880s-1900s), Internet Archive, as short wide tubes of rib or lace for covering the hair and neck. Cornelia Mee, A Manual of Knitting and Crochet (1846), Internet Archive, documents a ribbed snood construction.

glossaryTerms.definition: A rib pattern that alternates one knit stitch with one purl stitch on every row or round, producing a highly stretchy, reversible fabric.
A seaming technique that joins two parallel knitted edges invisibly from the right side by picking up the bars between stitches on each edge alternately. The seam is nearly invisible in rib fabric.
A cast-on forming a neat elastic edge by using the tail and working yarn over two fingers simultaneously.

content.text: This is a snood knitted flat in
1x1 rib

on 5 mm needles with worsted-weight yarn, seamed into a short wide tube, finishing at 70 cm circumference and 30 cm tall. The snood is worked as a flat rectangle and the two short edges are seamed together with
mattress stitch
to make the tube. The wide tube can be pulled up over the hair as a loose net or worn at the neck as a cowl.

Flat construction was chosen because a snood in 1x1 rib can be seamed invisibly with mattress stitch, which is easier for a beginner than joining a large-circumference tube in the round. The finished snood needs about 200 m (approximately 110 g) of worsted-weight yarn.
What you need

items.name: Worsted-weight wool or wool-blend yarn
items.substitutions: Any worsted-weight yarn. The rib stretch means a range of head sizes can wear the same snood.

items.name: 5 mm needles, straight or circular (UK 6 / US 8)
items.qty: 1 pair or 1 circular 60 cm or longer

content.text: Gauge

18 sts x 24 rows = 10 x 10 cm in stocking stitch on 5 mm needles, blocked. In 1x1 rib relaxed the gauge is approximately 14 sts per 10 cm because the rib compresses. Measure the swatch unstretched. The rib stretches to approximately 20 sts per 10 cm when fully extended. One stitch per 10 cm off gauge shifts the finished flat width by about 7 cm, which adds or removes about 14 cm of circumference once seamed and relaxed.
Stitches used
K (knit): right needle from left to right through front of stitch, wrap yarn counterclockwise, draw loop through.
P (purl): right needle from right to left through front of stitch with yarn in front, wrap yarn, draw loop through to back.
Pattern
Cast on
Use the
long-tail cast-on

to place 100 stitches on the needle. The stitch count is an even number for 1x1 rib; 100 stitches in 1x1 rib relaxed gives approximately 71 cm flat (= 35 cm relaxed width x 2) which seams to a 70 cm circumference. Before beginning, calculate the tail: tail_cm = (needle circumference mm x stitch count) / 10 + 15. For 5 mm needles (circumference approximately 15.7 mm) and 100 stitches: (15.7 x 100) / 10 + 15 = 157 + 15 = 172 cm. Leave a tail of at least 172 cm.
Stitch count check-in: after the cast-on you should have 100 stitches on the needle.
Body
Row 1 (RS): *K1, P1; repeat from * to end. (100 sts)
Row 2 (WS): *P1, K1; repeat from * to end. (100 sts)
Repeat rows 1 and 2 until the piece measures 30 cm from the cast-on edge. At the halfway mark (approximately row 33 of 66 body rows), count your stitches.
Stitch count check-in: at row 33 you should have 100 stitches on the needle.
Bind off

Work a stretchy bind-off in rib pattern: work each stitch in pattern (K the knit stitches, P the purl stitches) using the K2tog-tbl method on alternate stitches. The bound-off edge must match the cast-on edge stretch for the seamed tube to sit evenly.
Seaming

With RS facing, join the two short ends of the rectangle using mattress stitch: hold the two selvedge edges parallel and pick up the bar between the first and second stitches on each edge alternately. Pull the seaming yarn gently as you go to close the seam without puckering. The 1x1 rib seams nearly invisibly if the selvedge stitches on each edge match the same rib column.
Common faults

Rib columns misaligned at the seam. When lining up the two short edges for seaming, count the rib columns from each edge to confirm the K columns face K columns and P columns face P columns. A one-stitch misalignment breaks the rib pattern at the seam and looks obvious in use.
Seam puckering or tighter than the body. Mattress stitch should be worked at the same tension as the knitted fabric. If the seam puckers, ease the seaming yarn more gently along the edge as you work.
Bound-off edge narrower than cast-on. A standard bind-off on 1x1 rib loses elasticity. Always use a stretchy bind-off or bind off on a needle two sizes larger.
Finishing
Weave in the cast-on tail and the bind-off tail at the seam. Weave in the seaming tail. The snood does not need blocking.
Care
Handwash in cool water with wool wash. Lay flat over a round form to dry. Do not stretch the rib while wet.
What to try next

The ribbed cowl is the same rib tube worked in the round, which avoids the seam entirely. The ear-warming neckwarmer is a narrower tube that sits specifically at the base of the head and covers the ears.
